Foundations: How Adults Learn and How a ToT Works

Before you can train other trainers, you need a clear picture of what a Training-of-Trainers is, why cascades succeed or fail, and how adults actually learn. This module covers the cascade model, Knowles' principles of adult learning, Kolb's experiential learning cycle, and how to prepare a safe, inclusive training space.
What a Training-of-Trainers is and how the cascade works

A normal training teaches people a skill they will use themselves: bookkeeping, hand washing, savings group rules, safe food handling. A **Training-of-Trainers (ToT)** teaches people two things at once: the skill itself, and **how to teach that skill to others**. Graduates of a ToT go back to their communities, churches, cooperatives or women's groups and run the same training there.
A woman teaching a small group in front of a board
In a ToT you learn the content and also practise teaching it, so you can lead your own group afterwards.

This is why NGOs, government agencies, faith groups and networks like WODDI use ToTs. One small team of experienced trainers cannot reach every village or market. But if they train 20 people properly, and each of those 20 trains 25 more, the message reaches 500 people. This chain is called a **cascade**.

Why cascades lose quality

Every time knowledge passes from one level to the next, some of it can be lost, changed or simplified. Trainers and researchers call this **dilution** or the "watering down" effect. Think of the game where one person whispers a sentence to the next person in a line. By the tenth person, the sentence has changed. A cascade without good materials and follow-up can behave the same way.

Dilution happens for predictable reasons: the ToT was too short for trainers to practise, there was no written trainer guide, trainers were chosen because of status rather than skill, or nobody checked the first trainings at the next level. The good news is that each cause has a fix.
**A written trainer guide** with the exact key messages, activities and timings, so every trainer teaches the same core content.
**Practice inside the ToT**: every trainer teaches at least one real session and receives feedback before she leaves.
**Selection by criteria**: choose trainers who know the topic, communicate well and have time to train, not only those with titles.
**Follow-up support**: a master trainer observes or calls in on early sessions and answers questions on a WhatsApp group.
**Simple evaluation tools**: the same short test and feedback form used at every level, so you can see where quality drops.

Worked example: planning the reach of a cascade
For example, Amaka coordinates a women's network in Anambra. She wants to teach basic record keeping to market women in six local government areas within three months.
She selects 18 trainers, three per local government area, using criteria: can read and write, keeps her own business records, and is trusted in her market.
She plans a three-day ToT, with day three given almost entirely to practice teaching and feedback.
Each trainer agrees to run two sessions of about 15 women each within six weeks. Reach: 18 trainers x 2 sessions x 15 women = 540 women.
She builds in quality checks: she will personally observe one session in each local government area (six visits) and every trainer sends attendance lists and test scores to a WhatsApp group.
She plans for drop-out honestly: if only 15 of the 18 trainers complete both sessions, reach is 15 x 2 x 15 = 450 women.
Amaka sets a realistic target of 450 to 540 women and protects quality with practice, a trainer guide, observation and shared evaluation forms.
Smaller and stronger beats bigger and weaker

A ToT of 15 to 25 participants usually allows everyone to practise teaching and receive feedback. With 50 participants, most people only watch. If funders push for larger numbers, run two smaller ToTs instead of one big one.
A ToT is not a lecture about training

Participants in a ToT should spend much of their time doing what they will later do: practising sessions, giving feedback, running activities and using evaluation forms. If your ToT agenda is mostly presentations, rebalance it so that at least a third of the time is practice teaching.

Adults are not big children sitting in a classroom. They come with years of experience, responsibilities at home and work, and limited time. If a session feels irrelevant, they stop listening, or politely stop coming. Two ideas from adult education help you design sessions that adults value: **Malcolm Knowles' principles of andragogy** and **David Kolb's experiential learning cycle**.

Notice what this means in practice: less time reading slides, more time solving real problems. A market woman who has run a business for 15 years already knows a great deal about customers and credit. Your job is to connect new tools to what she already knows.
Kolb's experiential learning cycle
David Kolb described learning as a cycle with four stages, published in his 1984 book *Experiential Learning*. Learners can enter at any point, but a full learning experience passes through all four.
Concrete experience
Reflective observation
Abstract conceptualisation
Active experimentation
Do something, think about it, draw a general lesson, then try it again in a new way.
**Concrete experience**: learners do something or experience a situation (a role play, a demonstration, a short case story).
**Reflective observation**: they look back at what happened. What did you notice? How did it feel?
**Abstract conceptualisation**: they draw out the general idea, rule or model. What does this teach us? This is where your short input fits.
**Active experimentation**: they apply the idea to a new situation or plan how they will use it at home or in business.

Many trainers spend almost all their time in the third stage, explaining concepts. Adults then nod politely, go home, and nothing changes. When you design every main session to include an experience, a reflection, a short concept, and an application, learning sticks far better.
Worked example: one 45-minute session through all four stages
For example, Halima is training cooperative members in Kaduna on separating business money from household money.
Concrete experience (10 minutes): two volunteers act out a short role play. A trader takes money from her sales box for school fees and cooking gas, then cannot restock on market day.
Reflective observation (10 minutes): in pairs, members answer: What went wrong? Has this happened to you or someone you know?
Abstract conceptualisation (10 minutes): Halima presents one simple rule: keep two separate purses or accounts, and pay yourself a fixed amount each week from the business.
Active experimentation (15 minutes): each member decides the weekly amount she will pay herself and writes it down, then shares with a partner who will check in with her next week.
In 45 minutes, members moved from a familiar problem to a personal commitment. Halima only spoke for about 10 minutes, but the whole session was purposeful.
About 'learning styles'

You may hear that each person has one fixed learning style and must be taught only that way. Reviews of the research have not found good evidence for matching teaching to a single style. It is better to use variety: speaking, showing, doing and discussing in every session.
Using the cycle in a ToT

In a Training-of-Trainers, Kolb's cycle works on two levels. First, your trainees experience sessions built on the cycle as participants. Second, you pause and ask them to look at the design itself: "Which part of that session was the experience? Where did we reflect? When did I give the concept?" This makes the method visible, so they can copy it when they train others.

Good reflection questions move from what happened, to why it matters, to what next. A simple sequence many facilitators use is: **What?** (What happened? What did you notice?), **So what?** (What does this mean? Why does it matter?), and **Now what?** (What will you do differently?). These three questions fit naturally into the reflection and experimentation stages and are easy for new trainers to remember.

In the next lesson you will prepare the physical and social space where these sessions happen, because even a well-designed session fails if people cannot hear, feel unsafe, or are worried about their children outside.

People learn when they feel safe, comfortable and respected. A hot, crowded hall with no water, a trainer who arrives late, or a phone camera pointed at someone without permission can damage trust before you teach anything. Good trainers prepare the space as carefully as the content.
A person preparing materials and checking a list
Preparing the venue, materials and rules the day before saves you from avoidable problems.
Venue and logistics
**Seating**: arrange chairs in a horseshoe or small circles, not rows, so people can see each other and talk.
**Light, air and noise**: check fans, windows and whether a generator, church service or market noise will drown you out.
**Power**: if you need a projector or speaker, plan for power cuts. Have printed flip chart sheets as backup.
**Water and toilets**: confirm clean toilets and drinking water. Long sessions need a break every 60 to 90 minutes.
**Timing**: choose times that suit women's real schedules, for example after the morning market or after school drop-off.
Materials kit

A simple trainer kit works anywhere: flip chart paper, thick markers in several colours, masking tape, sticky notes or cut paper, a timer (your phone works), printed handouts, the attendance sheet, consent forms, pens for participants, and the trainer guide. Pack it the night before and tick each item.

Ground rules and safety

In the first 15 minutes, ask the group to suggest ground rules and write them on a flip chart. Common ones: phones on silent, one person speaks at a time, respect different views, what is shared personally stays in the room, start and end on time. Rules the group makes itself are easier to keep than rules you impose.
Consent for photos and personal data

Always ask before taking photos, and offer a clear option to say no without explanation. Use a short consent form that says what the photo or data is for and where it will be shared. Nigeria's Data Protection Act (2023) requires personal data to be collected for a clear purpose, kept secure and not shared beyond that purpose. Keep attendance lists with phone numbers in a safe place, not in a public WhatsApp group.
Inclusion from the start
**Language**: agree in advance whether to train in English, Pidgin, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or another local language, and arrange an interpreter if needed.
**Literacy**: use pictures, symbols, demonstrations and oral summaries so women who read little can fully take part.
**Disability**: choose a ground floor venue where possible, seat people with hearing or sight difficulties near the front, and ask privately what support each person needs.
**Childcare**: if mothers will bring babies, plan a corner or a helper so they can still participate.
**Transport and cost**: be clear in the invitation about whether transport is refunded, so nobody is embarrassed on the day.
Worked example: fixing a venue problem the day before
For example, Bisi is running a two-day ToT for 20 women leaders in a church hall in Ibadan. On her readiness check the evening before, she finds problems.
The hall has rows of fixed benches. She arranges to use the smaller side room with movable plastic chairs and sets up four circles of five.
There is no generator on weekdays. She drops the projector plan and prepares six flip chart sheets with the key diagrams instead.
Two participants use walking sticks. She confirms the side room is on the ground floor with no steps.
Three women said they will bring babies. She asks a youth volunteer to supervise a play mat in the corner where mothers can see their children.
She counts printed consent forms: 20 needed, plus five spare.
On the day, the session starts on time, everyone can see and move, and nobody is excluded. Bisi notes the changes in her trainer log for next time.
The first 15 minutes

The opening shapes the whole day. Arrive at least 45 minutes early to set up, so you can greet people at the door rather than arranging chairs while they wait. Start with a short welcome, introductions that link to the topic (for example, "Say your name and one thing you sell"), the purpose of the day, the agenda with break times, and the ground rules. Keep the attendance sheet near the door, and explain the consent form before anyone signs it, reading it aloud for those who prefer.
Electrical and crowd safety

Check extension cables for damage, keep them away from walkways and water, and do not overload one socket with a projector, speaker and phone chargers. Know where the exits are, keep them clear, and do not pack more people into a room than it can safely hold.
As a ToT trainer, you will teach these same preparation habits to your trainees. Include a readiness checklist in their trainer guide so every local session starts well.

Quick needs analysis

Analysis does not need to be expensive. Talk to five to ten future participants and two or three people who know their work (a cooperative chair, a market leader, a health worker). Ask what tasks they find hard, what mistakes happen often, and what they already do well. Also ask a hard question: **is training the real solution?** If women cannot save because there is no safe place to keep money, a session on saving will not fix that. Training fixes gaps in knowledge and skill, not missing tools or money.
Bloom's taxonomy: choosing the right level

Benjamin Bloom and colleagues published a taxonomy of learning objectives in 1956. A revised version by Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl (2001) uses six levels, from simple recall to creating something new. Each level has action verbs you can observe.

Avoid unmeasurable verbs
Verbs like "know", "understand", "appreciate" or "be aware of" cannot be observed. You cannot see someone "know" something. Replace them with what she will say, write, calculate or do.
Making objectives SMART

A good learning objective is **Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound**. In training, the time part is usually "by the end of the session". A simple formula: **By the end of [time], participants will be able to [Bloom's verb] [task] [to what standard].**
Worked example: from vague aim to SMART objectives
For example, Chioma is designing a half-day training for 25 women who sell cooked food at a motor park in Owerri. Her first draft aim was: "Participants will understand food hygiene."
Analysis: she talks to eight sellers and the park's welfare officer. The main gaps: not washing hands after handling money, keeping cooked food uncovered, and reusing dirty water.
She checks that training is the right fix: soap and covers are affordable, so the gap is habits and knowledge, not missing tools.
Objective 1 (Apply): By the end of the session, participants will be able to demonstrate correct hand washing with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds.
Objective 2 (Understand): By the end of the session, participants will be able to explain two ways uncovered food becomes contaminated.
Objective 3 (Create): By the end of the session, each participant will be able to draw up a three-step daily hygiene routine for her own stall.
Each objective is observable and can be checked before the women leave: a hand washing demonstration, a short verbal explanation, and a written or drawn routine.

Write objectives before you write any content or activities. Then, in the Development phase, check every handout and activity against them. If an activity does not help learners reach an objective, it is decoration. Objectives also become your test questions later: an objective that says "calculate interest" needs a test item where learners actually calculate interest.
In a ToT, share your objectives with trainees and ask them to check each local session against the same objectives, so every level of the cascade aims at the same result.
Three to five objectives are enough for a half-day session. More than that usually means you are trying to cover too much, which is one of the most common reasons community trainings run over time.

A **session plan** is the trainer's map. It lists each part of the session, how long it takes, what the trainer does, what participants do, and what materials are needed. In a ToT, session plans are essential: they are what your trainees carry home, and they are your best protection against dilution.
A person planning a schedule on a calendar
A session plan turns objectives into a timed sequence anyone can follow.
The parts of a strong session
**Opening (about 10 percent of time)**: welcome, purpose, objectives in plain words, link to what learners already know.
**Experience or activity**: a role play, demonstration, case story or problem that gets people involved early.
**Reflection and discussion**: pairs or small groups talk about what happened and share with the room.
**Short input**: the key concept, rule or method, usually 10 to 15 minutes at a time.
**Practice**: learners apply the method themselves, with the trainer moving around to help.
**Check and close**: a quick check against the objectives, a summary, and one action each person will take.
Plan **one objective per main block**, and check each block with a question: does this activity help participants reach the objective? If not, cut it, even if it is interesting.

Worked example: fitting content into the time you really have
For example, Fatima has a three-hour slot (180 minutes) with a women's cooperative in Kano. Her first plan has 230 minutes of activities.
She first protects realistic overhead: 15 minutes for late arrivals and settling, and a 20-minute break. That leaves 145 minutes of teaching time.

She keeps her three objectives and lists every activity under one of them. Two activities support no objective: a long history of cooperatives (25 minutes) and a second icebreaker (15 minutes). She cuts both.
Now the plan is 190 minutes, still 45 over her 145. She shortens her input on record keeping from 35 to 15 minutes and uses a printed handout instead.
She reduces group reports from 30 to 15 minutes by asking only two groups to report and others to add anything new.
Final plan: 130 minutes of activities, leaving a 15-minute buffer for questions or delays.
Fatima's plan now fits 145 minutes with a 15-minute buffer, covers all three objectives, and keeps practice time intact, which is where most learning happens.
Always have a plan B

Mark one activity in your plan as optional, so you can drop it if you run late. Mark another as a stretch activity in case a fast group finishes early. Write both into the trainer guide so your trainees can do the same.

Timing estimates improve with experience. After each session, write the actual time each block took beside the planned time. After two or three sessions you will plan much more accurately, and you can share these real timings with the trainers you train.
Energy across the day

Attention drops after a heavy lunch and late in the afternoon. Put active work, such as practice, role plays and gallery walks, in those slots, and keep short inputs for the morning when people are fresh. A quick energiser of two or three minutes (standing up, a clapping game, a quick quiz) can rescue a tired room, but choose energisers that suit the age, culture and physical ability of the group. Nobody should feel embarrassed or excluded.

For a full-day ToT, repeat the same structure across several sessions and end the day with a short review: what did we learn today, what is still unclear, and what will we do tomorrow? Write the unclear points on a flip chart and start the next morning by answering them.
Keep the language plain

Write session plans in the language and style your trainees will use. If a trainer will deliver in Hausa or Pidgin, translate the key messages and questions in advance, rather than asking her to translate on the spot.

Asking good questions

Closed questions ("Did you understand?") get a yes and tell you nothing. Open questions start with what, how, why or tell me about: "What would you do if a member missed two repayments?" After asking, **wait**. Count silently to five before rephrasing. Silence gives quieter people time to think.
**Dominant participant**: thank her, then say "Let us hear from someone who has not spoken yet." Give her a role, such as timekeeper.
**Quiet participant**: use pairs first, so she can rehearse with one person. Ask her group, not her alone, to report.
**Off-topic question**: write it on a "parking lot" sheet and promise to return to it at the break.
**Disagreement**: welcome it, ask each side for their reasons, and link back to the evidence or the objective.
Microteaching

**Microteaching** is a short practice teaching session, usually 10 to 15 minutes, delivered to a small group of fellow trainees who then give feedback. It is the most important part of a ToT, because trainers learn to teach by teaching, not by listening to talks about teaching.
The microteaching cycle

Teach to peers
Receive feedback
Re-plan
Re-teach
Teaching the same segment twice, with feedback in between, shows each trainer how much she can improve.
Giving useful feedback

Feedback should be **specific, about behaviour (not personality), balanced and actionable**. Two simple models work well in community settings. The first is **What went well / Even better if**: name two things that worked and one clear improvement. The second is **Situation-Behaviour-Impact (SBI)**, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership: describe when it happened, what the person did, and the effect it had.
Worked example: a microteaching round in a ToT
For example, in a ToT in Jos, Rahila teaches a 12-minute segment on filling a savings passbook to five peers. Her co-trainer Esther leads the feedback.
Rahila states her objective: "By the end, you will be able to record a deposit in the passbook correctly."
She demonstrates once, then asks everyone to record a 5,000 naira deposit. Two peers make mistakes in the balance column.
Feedback, what went well: "Your objective was clear, and you got everyone practising within five minutes."
Feedback, SBI: "When you checked the practice sheets (situation), you corrected the errors yourself (behaviour), so the two learners did not find out why they were wrong (impact)."
Even better if: "Ask the learner to check her balance against the sample first, then explain."
Rahila re-plans and re-teaches the next day. This time both struggling peers find their own errors.
Rahila improves one specific skill, guiding learners to correct their own mistakes, in under 30 minutes of practice and feedback.

Receiving feedback is a skill too. Teach trainees to listen without defending themselves, write down what they hear, ask a clarifying question if needed ("Can you give me an example?"), and thank the person. They then choose one or two points to work on, rather than trying to fix everything at once. In a ToT, model this yourself by asking participants for feedback on your own sessions at the end of each day.

When planning microteaching, divide trainees into groups of four to six with one experienced trainer or a trained peer as the feedback lead. Give each trainee a different segment of the real curriculum, so the whole training is rehearsed by the group, and keep strict time: about 10 to 15 minutes teaching and 10 minutes feedback each.

The person who taught speaks first about what she noticed. Peers then give one strength and one improvement each. No one comments on voice, accent, appearance or dress. Feedback is about teaching behaviour only.

Quality, Ethics and Evaluation

Running a training once is not enough; it has to be good every time, safe for everyone, and proven to work. This module covers quality standards and common mistakes, ethics and safeguarding in community training, and how to evaluate results with Kirkpatrick's four levels and report them clearly.

Fidelity and adaptation

**Fidelity** means delivering a training as designed: the same key messages, activities and checks. In a cascade, fidelity matters because a trainer who changes the key messages may spread wrong information. But some adaptation is healthy: changing a case story so it fits farmers rather than traders, or delivering in Yoruba instead of English.

A useful rule for your trainer guide: mark content as **core** (must not change: facts, safety rules, key steps, the test) or **flexible** (can adapt: examples, names in stories, energisers, language). Trainers then know what they may adjust.

Co-facilitation

Pairing trainers improves quality. Before the session, agree who leads which block, who keeps time, and a signal for "we are running late". During the session, the supporting trainer watches the room, helps groups and notes questions. After the session, take 10 minutes to debrief: what worked, what to change. New trainers learn fast when paired with experienced ones.

Quality also depends on who is selected as a trainer. Agree selection criteria with the community or organisation in advance, write them down and apply them openly. When people see that trainers are chosen for knowledge, communication skills and commitment rather than family or political ties, they trust the training more and participants take it more seriously.

Finally, quality needs time. A ToT squeezed into one afternoon cannot give each trainer practice and feedback. When planning with partners, protect enough days for the content, microteaching for every trainer, and a short session on how to use the evaluation tools, even if that means training fewer trainers at first.
Keep a trainer log

After every session, write the date, place, number of participants, what went well, what you would change, and actual timings. A notebook or phone note is enough. Over time it becomes powerful evidence of your growth.

Ethics, inclusion and safeguarding in community training
Apply the principle of do no harm when planning a training
Handle personal stories, personal data and money transparently
Make sessions accessible to women with low literacy or disabilities

Trainers hold power. Participants may look up to you, depend on you for transport refunds or certificates, or share personal stories during discussions. With that power comes responsibility. Ethical training protects participants, protects your reputation, and protects the organisation you work with.
A shield protecting a person and their information
Protecting participants' safety, dignity and data is part of the trainer's job.
Do no harm

Before a training, ask: could anything in this session put someone at risk? Examples: a discussion of money that makes a woman's husband suspicious, a role play about conflict that reopens painful memories, or a group photo that reveals someone's location. Design to reduce these risks, for example by using fictional case stories instead of asking for personal experiences on sensitive topics.
Confidentiality and personal data
Agree in the ground rules that personal stories shared in the room are not repeated outside it.
Collect only the personal data you need. If you only need numbers for a report, do not collect home addresses.
Explain why you are collecting phone numbers or test scores and who will see them.
Store attendance lists and forms securely: a locked bag or folder, or a password-protected phone or file.
Report results as totals or averages, not named individuals, unless someone has given permission.

These habits match the principles of Nigeria's Data Protection Act (2023), enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission: personal data should be collected for a clear purpose, limited to what is necessary, kept secure, and not used for other purposes without consent.
Money and transparency

Transport refunds, lunch and materials are common sources of conflict and mistrust. State clearly in the invitation what will be provided. Pay or refund in the same way for everyone, record every payment with a signature or transfer receipt, and never ask participants for money to receive a certificate unless this was openly agreed in advance. Where possible, use bank transfer or a mobile money app so there is a record.

Inclusion is not only about who is invited, but whether each person can fully take part. Use oral instructions as well as written ones, read handouts aloud, and use symbols or colours on forms. For evaluation, replace written tests with picture-based questions or short oral checks when literacy is low. Ask privately, for example on the registration form, whether anyone needs support to participate.
If someone discloses harm

Sometimes a participant shares that she or her child is being harmed. Listen calmly, do not push for details, and do not promise to keep a secret you may need to report. Thank her for telling you, explain what you can and cannot do, and follow your organisation's safeguarding procedure by informing the named safeguarding focal person promptly. Never investigate on your own. Before any training, find out who that focal person is and which local support services exist.
Worked example: planning an ethical, inclusive session
For example, Zainab is preparing a ToT on household budgeting for 20 women in a community near Maiduguri. Several participants do not read, and the topic touches family finances.
She replaces 'share your own family budget' with a fictional case story of a woman called Laraba, so nobody has to reveal personal income.
She designs a picture-based budget sheet using symbols for food, school fees, transport and savings, so women who do not read can use it.
Her registration form asks only for name, phone number and any support needs, and explains the data is for follow-up calls only.

She budgets 1,500 naira per person for transport (an approximate local figure for this example), pays by transfer where possible, and records cash payments with a thumbprint where someone cannot sign.
She confirms with her organisation who the safeguarding focal person is and writes the contact in her trainer guide.
Zainab's session protects privacy, includes non-readers fully, keeps money transparent and is ready if a sensitive disclosure happens.

Respect also shows in small things: using people's preferred names and titles, not singling out anyone's mistakes in front of the group, scheduling around prayer times and market days, and making sure older women and younger women both get a chance to speak. These habits make the training room a place where women feel safe enough to try new skills and admit what they do not yet know.

When you train other trainers, include these ethics practices in the ToT itself, through a short case discussion such as: "A participant asks you to lend her money. What do you do?" Practising these situations before they happen builds good judgement.

How do you know your training worked? "People enjoyed it" is a start, but it is not proof that anything changed. **Kirkpatrick's four levels**, first described by Donald Kirkpatrick in the late 1950s, are the most widely used framework for evaluating training. Each level answers a different question.

Level 1 and 2 tools

For reaction, keep the form short: three to five questions such as "How useful was today for your work?" on a 1 to 5 scale, plus "What will you use first?" and "What should we change?" For low-literacy groups, use smiley faces and ask the open questions orally.

For learning, use the **same short test before and after** the session, five to ten questions linked directly to your objectives. Skill objectives are best checked by watching a demonstration with a simple checklist. Calculate the average score before and after, and the change.
Worked example: calculating learning gain and follow-up
For example, Ngozi runs a record keeping training for 20 traders in Onitsha with a 10-question pre-test and post-test, and follows up six weeks later.
Pre-test: the 20 scores add up to 80, so the average is 80 / 20 = 4.0 out of 10 (40 percent).
Post-test: the scores add up to 160, so the average is 160 / 20 = 8.0 out of 10 (80 percent).
Change: 8.0 - 4.0 = 4.0 points, an increase of 40 percentage points. 17 of 20 traders scored 7 or above after training, compared with 2 before.
Reaction: average usefulness rating 4.6 out of 5. Most common request: more practice time.
Behaviour, six weeks later: she calls all 20 and reaches 18. Of these, 12 say they record sales daily, and she sees photos of record books from 9 of them.

Ngozi can report strong learning (40 to 80 percent) and early behaviour change (12 of the 18 reached are recording daily), while honestly noting that 9 confirmations are backed by photos and the rest are self-reported.
Be honest about what the numbers show

A higher post-test score shows learning, not business growth. Self-reported behaviour may be higher than real behaviour. State how many people you reached at follow-up and how you checked. Honest reports build more trust with funders than impressive claims.
Behaviour and results

Level 3 is where most trainings fall silent, yet it is often what funders and communities care about most. Plan it before training starts: decide what behaviour you expect, how you will check it (call, visit, photo of a record book), and when. Level 4 results, such as increased group savings or fewer food hygiene complaints, usually need records kept over months and are influenced by many factors besides training, so describe your contribution carefully rather than claiming the training alone caused them.
A one-page evaluation report
**What**: training title, dates, place, trainers, number of participants (and how many were women, youth or persons with disabilities if relevant).
**Objectives**: the three to five learning objectives.
**Results by level**: reaction average, pre and post averages, behaviour follow-up findings.
**What worked and what we will change**: two or three points each.
**Evidence and limits**: how data was collected, how many were followed up, what was self-reported.

Keep evaluation light enough that trainers will actually do it. A five-question reaction form, a ten-question test and three follow-up questions by phone are enough for most community trainings. Agree in advance who collects the forms, who enters the scores (a simple spreadsheet or exercise book is fine), and when the report is due. In a cascade, use exactly the same tools at every level so you can compare results between trainers and spot where quality is dropping.
Share results back with participants too. Telling a group "most of you improved from 4 to 8 out of 10" builds confidence and encourages them to keep using the skill.

Paid, partly paid or volunteer

Not every training will be paid. Many community sessions are voluntary. Still, cost them fully, so that partners see the real value, and so you can ask a funder or sponsor to cover the costs. When payment is involved, use a transfer or a payment link such as Paystack and always issue a receipt.
Building trust with partners

Agree in writing, even in a short email or WhatsApp message, what you will deliver, the dates, the number of participants, the payment terms and the report you will send. Send your report on time, even when results are mixed. Partners return to trainers who are reliable and honest, and a satisfied partner often recommends you to others.

Different partners need different levels of detail. A funder may want a full budget table and evaluation plan; a women's fellowship leader may only need the dates, the topic, what members will be able to do, and what it will cost. Prepare a one-page version and a short three-line version for WhatsApp, and offer the full detail on request.

If a partner offers less money than your budget, do not simply cut your fee in silence. Show the options: fewer participants, fewer printed materials, a shorter session, or a sponsor to cover part of the cost. Protect practice time and follow-up, because those produce the results the partner wants to see.

When you present results, lead with the change in what people can do, then the numbers that show it, then the evidence and its limits. For example: "After training, 17 of 20 traders could complete a daily sales record correctly, up from 2 before. Six weeks later, 12 of 18 reached said they record daily, and 9 shared photos." That is clear, specific and honest.

Worked example: a realistic 90-day plan
For example, Blessing has completed the course and wants to cascade her savings group record keeping training through her church's women's fellowship in Port Harcourt.
Days 1 to 30: deliver her training twice to 20 women each (40 in total), using her revised package. Record reaction and pre and post test data.

Keep supporting your trainers

Create a WhatsApp group for your trainers to share questions, photos (with consent) and attendance lists. Hold a short check-in call every two weeks. New trainers are most likely to drift from the guide in their first few sessions, so that is when your support matters most.
Growing as a trainer

Trainers who keep improving tend to share three habits. They seek feedback after every session, not only when something goes wrong. They watch other trainers and borrow good techniques. And they keep evidence: logs, scores and reflections that show progress over time. Set yourself one improvement goal per month, for example "ask more open questions" or "finish every session on time", and review it in your trainer log.

As you start training other trainers, your role shifts towards that of a master trainer. You will spend more time designing materials, observing, coaching and checking quality, and less time delivering every session yourself. Plan for this in your 90-day plan by blocking out time for observation visits and check-in calls, not just for your own sessions.

Look after yourself as well. Training is tiring work, especially with travel, heat and long days. Build rest days into your plan, share the load with co-facilitators, and do not accept more sessions than you can deliver well. A trainer who is exhausted cannot give participants her best.

At day 90, compare what happened with what you planned: reach, test results, observation scores and follow-up findings. Note what you will keep, change or stop, and set your next 90-day goals from that review.

Keep learning too. Ask to co-facilitate with more experienced trainers, observe others, and keep your trainer log. Each training you deliver and evaluate makes your portfolio stronger and your cascade more reliable.

What a ToT is
Teach the skill and how to teach it

The main risk: dilution, or watering down
A normal training teaches a skill people use themselves. A Training-of-Trainers, or ToT, teaches two things at once: the skill, and how to teach that skill to others.
Graduates go back to their churches, cooperatives and women's groups and run the same training there.
One small team cannot reach every village. But train 20 people properly, and if each trains 25 more, the message reaches 500 people. This chain is called a cascade.
The risk is dilution. Like a whispered sentence passed down a line, the message can change at each level unless you protect it.
Stop the watering down
Five fixes for dilution
A written trainer guide with key messages
Every trainer practises a real session
Choose trainers by criteria, not status
Follow-up: observe early sessions
The same short test at every level
Give every trainer a written guide with the exact key messages, activities and timings.
Make every trainer teach at least one real session inside the ToT, and get feedback before she leaves. At least a third of a ToT should be practice teaching.
Choose trainers who know the topic, communicate well and have time, not only those with titles.
Observe or call in on early sessions, and answer questions on a WhatsApp group.
And use the same short test and feedback form at every level, so you can see where quality drops.

18 trainers, three per local government area

After a three-day ToT, each trainer agrees to run two sessions of about 15 women within six weeks.

She plans honestly for drop-out. If only 15 trainers finish, the reach is 450. So her target is 450 to 540, protected by observation visits and shared forms.

Malcolm Knowles described how adults learn. They need to know why. They bring years of experience. They want help with real problems, and they see themselves as responsible for their own decisions.

Kolb's cycle
One 45-minute session, four stages
Keep your own talking to a short part of each session.
Experience: a role play (10 minutes)
Reflect: what went wrong? (10 minutes)
Concept: one simple rule (10 minutes)
Experiment: a personal plan (15 minutes)
David Kolb described learning as a cycle: experience, reflect, draw the lesson, then try it. For example, Halima teaches cooperative members in Kaduna to separate business money from household money.
First, 10 minutes of experience. Two volunteers act out a trader who takes school fees from her sales box, then cannot restock.
Then 10 minutes to reflect in pairs. What went wrong? Has this happened to you?
Then 10 minutes for the concept: keep two separate purses, and pay yourself a fixed amount each week.
Finally, 15 minutes to experiment. Each woman writes her weekly amount and tells a partner who will check in.
Halima only spoke for about 10 minutes. Many trainers spend all their time explaining, and nothing changes. Use the cycle, and learning sticks.

The session plan
Parts of a strong session
Every activity must support an objective, or it goes.
Opening: purpose and objectives
Experience: role play or case story
Reflection in pairs or small groups
Short input: 10 to 15 minutes
Practice, with the trainer moving round

A session plan is the trainer's map: time, activity, what the trainer does, what participants do, and materials. In a ToT, it is your best protection against dilution.
Open with the purpose and objectives in plain words.
Get people involved early with a role play, demonstration or case story.
Let pairs or small groups talk about what happened.
Give a short input, usually 10 to 15 minutes at a time.
Then practice, with you moving round to help.
Close with a quick check against the objectives, and one action each person will take.
Ask of every block: does this help them reach an objective? If not, cut it, even if it is interesting.
Worked example
Fitting the time you really have
180-minute slot, but 230 minutes planned
Protect 15 minutes settling, 20-minute break
Cut two activities with no objective
Shorten input and group reports
130 minutes planned, 15-minute buffer
For example, Fatima has 180 minutes with a cooperative in Kano, but her first plan has 230 minutes of activities.
She protects 15 minutes for late arrivals and a 20-minute break. That leaves 145 minutes of teaching time.
A long history of cooperatives and a second icebreaker support no objective, so she cuts both.
She cuts her input from 35 to 15 minutes with a printed handout, and lets only two groups report.
Her final plan is 130 minutes, with a 15-minute buffer, and practice time stays intact. That is where most learning happens.

Handling the room
Thank her, invite someone who has not spoken, give her a role like timekeeper.
Use pairs first, and ask her group to report, not her alone.
Write it on a parking lot sheet and return to it at the break.
Ask open questions starting with what, how or why, and then wait. Count silently to five.

An off-topic question goes on a parking lot sheet, and you return to it at the break.

The teacher speaks first. Peers give one strength and one improvement each. No one comments on voice, accent or dress.

Quality
Weak session, strong session
Weak

Quality means participants reach the objectives and leave able to do something new. It does not mean beautiful slides.
A weak session is easy to spot in the first hour. The trainer talks most of the time, nobody practises, and it runs over.
In a strong session, participants are active, there are three to five clear objectives, they practise with coaching, and it ends on time with a check.
Fidelity
Core or flexible?
Core: facts, safety rules, key steps, the test. Never change these.
Mark each part of the guide core or flexible
Core stays: facts, safety, key steps, test
Flexible adapts: stories, names, language
Observe with a short scored checklist
Fidelity means delivering the training as designed. In a cascade, a trainer who changes key messages may spread wrong information. But some adaptation is healthy.
So mark every part of your trainer guide as core or flexible.
Core content must not change: facts, safety rules, key steps and the test.
Flexible content can adapt: examples, names in stories, energisers, and the language you teach in.
Then observe. Score seven items 0, 1 or 2. For example, Ifeoma observes Grace near Abakaliki and scores her 9 out of 14. Practice scored 0, because the history of savings groups took the time.
Ifeoma's feedback: even better if you cut the history and give 20 minutes to passbook practice. The history becomes flexible, and practice becomes core, for every trainer in the cascade.
Ethics and safeguarding
Trainers hold power
Collect only what you need, say why, store it securely, report totals not names.
Say what is provided. Pay everyone the same way and record every payment.
Listen calmly, no secret promises, tell the safeguarding focal person. Never investigate.
Do no harm. A money discussion could make a husband suspicious, so use a fictional case story instead of asking for personal experiences on sensitive topics.
Collect only the personal data you need, explain why, store it securely, and report totals, not names.
Transport refunds cause mistrust. Say clearly what is provided, pay everyone the same way, and record every payment with a signature, thumbprint or transfer receipt.

If a participant shares that she or her child is being harmed, listen calmly and do not push for details. Do not promise to keep a secret. Inform your safeguarding focal person promptly, and never investigate on your own.
Find out who that person is before every training.
Kirkpatrick
Four levels of evaluation
Reaction: was it useful? End of session
Learning: same test before and after
Behaviour: using it? 4 to 12 weeks later
Results: outcomes, 3 to 12 months later
People enjoyed it is a start, not proof. Level one is reaction: a short feedback form, with smiley faces for low-literacy groups.
Level two is learning: the same short test before and after, linked to your objectives.
Level three is behaviour: a follow-up call or visit 4 to 12 weeks later. Plan it before the training starts.
Level four is results, like savings totals, 3 to 12 months later. Many things affect results, so describe your contribution carefully.
Worked example
Calculating learning gain
Say how many you reached and how you checked. Honesty builds trust.
Pre-test: 80 / 20 = 4.0 out of 10
Post-test: 160 / 20 = 8.0 out of 10
Change: 40 percentage points
Six weeks later: 12 of 18 reached record daily
For example, Ngozi trains 20 traders in Onitsha with a 10-question test. Before training, the scores add up to 80. 80 divided by 20 is an average of 4.0 out of 10.
After training, the scores add up to 160. That is an average of 8.0 out of 10.
So the average went from 40 percent to 80 percent, an increase of 40 percentage points.
Six weeks later she calls all 20 and reaches 18. 12 say they record sales daily, and 9 send photos of their record books.
Ngozi reports this honestly: 9 are backed by photos, the rest are self-reported. A higher test score shows learning, not business growth.

Fictional cases for sensitive topics
Know your safeguarding focal person
Reaction, learning, behaviour, results

Mistakes are cheap in a pilot and expensive in a cascade.
Pilot with a small real group
For example, Adaeze designs a one-day training on safe grain storage for women farmers in Benue, and pilots it with 16 women.
The post-test average is only 6.0 out of 10, below her target of 7. Most women got the moisture questions wrong, and the demonstration was hard to see from the back.
So she runs the demonstration in three small groups, and gives moisture checking 20 more minutes of practice.
A second pilot gives 7.8 out of 10. Only then does she train 15 trainers.
Give every version a number and date, and make sure every trainer gets the latest one.
Winning partners
The need, from your needs analysis
What participants will be able to do
How: sessions, length, methods, language
How we will know it worked
Cost and what it covers
About the trainer: one past result
Partners do not buy sessions. They want changes in what people can do. So start with the need, then your SMART objectives.
Explain how you will train, and how you will know it worked: reaction, pre and post test, and a follow-up check.
Then the cost, and one result from a past training. For example: after training, 17 of 20 traders could complete a daily sales record, up from 2 before.
Worked example
Costing a one-day training
For example, Kemi costs a one-day record keeping training for 25 cooperative members.
Printing: 25 x 800
Refreshments: 25 x 1,500
Kemi's fee: 2 days x 25,000
Subtotal, all costs
Contingency, 10 percent
Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a worked example. Kemi is asked by a cooperative in Abeokuta to train 25 members for one day. The venue is free. All prices are approximate.
Printing is 25 times 800, which is 20,000 naira. Refreshments are 25 times 1,500, which is 37,500.
Her own fee covers a preparation day as well as the delivery day: 2 times 25,000, which is 50,000.
With flip chart and markers at 10,000, a co-facilitator at 15,000, and 5,000 for follow-up calls, the subtotal is 137,500.
She adds a 10 percent contingency for price changes: 13,750.
Total: 151,250 naira, or 6,050 per participant. She quotes about 151,000 and shows exactly what each amount covers.
Trust
Keep partners coming back
Deliverables, dates, numbers, payment terms and the report, even in a WhatsApp message.
Use a transfer or payment link and always issue a receipt.
Show options: fewer people or materials. Protect practice and follow-up.
Agree in writing what you will deliver, the dates, payment terms and the report. Then send the report on time, even when results are mixed.
When payment is involved, use a transfer or a payment link, and always issue a receipt.
If a partner offers less than your budget, do not cut your fee in silence. Show options, like fewer participants or a shorter session, but protect practice and follow-up.
Your plan
A realistic 90 days
Days 1 to 30: deliver twice to 20 women each
Days 31 to 60: train six trainers
Days 61 to 90: trainers reach about 90
Day 90: one-page report and review
For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt delivers her training twice to 20 women each, recording test data.
Next, she selects six trainers by clear criteria and runs a two-day ToT with microteaching.
Each trainer runs one session of about 15 women. Blessing observes three and calls the others. New trainers drift most in their first sessions.
At day 90 she reports reach, results and next steps. That is about 130 women, with quality checks at every level.
Key points
Test the guide on someone who missed the ToT
Pilot and revise before you scale
Cost everything, plus a contingency
Show problems and improvements honestly
Deliver, train trainers, follow up, report

To remember. Test your guide on someone new. Pilot before you scale. Cost everything, including preparation and follow-up, plus a contingency. Show problems and improvements honestly. And plan 90 days: deliver, multiply, follow up, report.
